title: How a Router Forwards a Packet: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: A packet arrives at a router. It has a split second to decide where it goes. Here's how it thinks.

lines.t: The router has a few seconds

scenes.heading: The sorting office
scenes.narration: A sorting office gets letters in an outer envelope addressed to the office itself. That's the frame, with the router's own M A C address. The worker opens the outer envelope and reads the inner address. That's the I P address. Then they check a giant wall chart, which is the routing table, for the best match. They put the letter in a new outer envelope for the next stop, and cross one off the lifetime count.

scenes.heading: Four steps
scenes.narration: Every hop runs the same four steps. Strip the old frame. Look up the destination in the table. Lower the T T L by one. And wrap it in a new frame for the next hop.

steps.title: Re-wrap in a new frame
steps.sub: New MAC for the next hop

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. Routers forward on the I P address, not the M A C. The T T L drops by exactly one at each router. And a router only uses a default route if you've configured one. Otherwise, it drops the packet.

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva the routing process lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A router strips the frame, looks up the I P address, and wraps a new frame. The T T L goes down by one at every hop. No matching route and no default means the packet is dropped. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva the routing process lab.

points.t: No route and no default = dropped
